Lviv Yanivske Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · L'vivs'ka oblast, Ukraine

Demolished. Lviv's Jewish community dates to the city's mid-13th-century founding, when both Jews and Karaites settled there; two distinct Jewish communities coexisted from the 14th through 19th centuries, sharing a cemetery that emerged in 1441. This cemetery, likely named for its proximity to the Janowska district — later the site of the notorious Janowska concentration camp, where 13,000 to 15,000 people perished during the Holocaust — was itself established in 1855. Lviv became a major center of Galician Hasidism, Haskalah, and Jewish printing, and by 1939 its Jewish population had reached 109,500 (33 percent of the city), swelling further with refugees from German-occupied Poland. Some 40,000 Jews were executed in a single wave in August 1941, with survivors confined to the Lviv Ghetto; only 3,400 Jews were registered in the city after liberation. The chess grandmaster Alexander Beliavsky and mathematician Mark Vishik were both born in Lviv.
